LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Harmony — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches harmony — what happens when a second note joins the tune and, instead of arguing, they agree: the warm, full sound underneath every great song.

What is this?

Harmony is notes sounding together on purpose: the melody sings on top, and one or more friendlier notes hum underneath, making the sound warm, full and rich. Solo = one voice; harmony = voices agreeing.

What does it mean?

Harmony is the musical version of teamwork: two different sounds choosing to fit. The ear hears the tune, but the chest feels the warmth underneath — and a child who can HEAR the underneath has learned to listen in layers.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three harmony ideas: harmony is at least TWO notes at once — the tune and its warm friend; the friend sits UNDER the tune and holds steady; and the test is the ear: agree, and it sounds rich; argue, and it sounds grumpy.

Why this matters

Layer-listening — melody above, harmony below — starts here and never stops: choirs, bands, film scores all live in layers. The family hum is the friendliest first harmony ever written.

What it teaches

Two-layer listening, pitch matching underneath a melody, steady holding while another moves (the harmony job), and agree-versus-grump discrimination.

Words to learn

harmonytogethermelodyunderneathwarmlayersagree

Say this to your child

“"Harmony is two notes agreeing! Sing a tune alone — lovely. Now a friend hums ONE steady note underneath — hear how the sound gets WARM and full? That is harmony: the tune dancing on top, the warm friend holding it up. And when the two notes argue — grumpy! — slide until they agree: rich!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is harmony — two notes agreeing to sound together."
  2. One voice, two voices: hum a tune alone. Now hum it WHILE a partner hums one steady low note underneath — hear the warmth bloom? That is harmony.
  3. The agree test: try a partner note that FIGHTS the tune — grumpy! Slide it until it fits — rich! The ear always knows.
  4. The harmony job: the tune moves; the harmony holds. Holding steady while another voice moves is a real musical skill — the anchor.
  5. Play the family harmony game below and close: "one tune, one warm friend."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Harmony" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly music illustration below — exactly as the agreeing notes look.

Ask your child

"How many notes make harmony? Where does the harmony friend sit — on top or underneath? What does the ear feel when they agree?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two notes, agreeing!" "The warm friend underneath!" or the anchor: "I hold steady while the tune dances!"

Out in the real world

Harmony hums under every chorus, every hymn, every lullaby sung by two people — and the fastest test is the family hum: one voice sings the tune, the rest hum one low note. The living room blooms.

Try it together

Family Harmony: one singer sings any simple tune (a favourite works); everyone else hums ONE steady low note underneath — the anchor. Listen for the moment the warmth blooms — agree! Then try the grumpy note ON PURPOSE: slide the anchor wrong, hear it fight, slide it home. Agree-versus-grump, felt in the chest. Two layers, one song, a family in harmony.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is harmony? What is the harmony note’s job? What happens when notes argue?" Notes together, hold steady underneath, it sounds grumpy — three answers and the warmth blooms.

Parent tips

Low and steady wins the harmony — anchors hum LOW. And the grumpy-note experiment is essential: hearing the FIGHT teaches the FIT better than any explanation.

This lesson pairs with the Harmony flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).
